title: Meta Ran Ads That Contained AI-Generated Child Sexual Abuse Imagery
gist: Tech Transparency Project researchers found more than 50 paid Meta ads over nine months containing explicit AI-generated child sexual abuse material and links to 'nudify' apps, some reaching thousands of accounts across the US, UK and Europe; Meta removed the ads only after WIRED's inquiry, and roughly 30 additional similar ads — some published after WIRED first contacted Meta — were found in a second sweep, undercutting the company's claims about its new AI-detection systems.

themes.theme: Scale and nature of the ad-network failure

insights.claim: Researchers at the Tech Transparency Project (TTP) found more than 50 image and video ads containing AI-generated child sexual abuse material running across Facebook, Instagram, Messenger and/or Threads over the prior nine months, with some ads linking out to 'nudify' or undressing apps; the ads were reviewed, approved, and run by Meta itself rather than posted by third parties as organic content.
insights.speaker: Katie Paul (via Matt Burgess)
insights.so_what: Because these were paid, Meta-reviewed and approved ads (not user-generated content Meta merely hosts), this represents a direct failure of Meta's own ad-review pipeline rather than a moderation gap on organic content — a materially higher liability and regulatory exposure category.
insights.quote: These ads made no effort to mask the images or hide what they were promoting. It's important to point out that this isn't content posted by third parties on Facebook or Instagram.
insights.locator: These ads made no effort to mask the images

insights.claim: The ads ran between November of last year and the start of August, often over periods of several days, with some specifically targeted at men; at least one ad reached 2,563 accounts across France, Germany, Ireland, Italy, the Netherlands, Spain, Sweden, and the UK, though Meta's ad library does not disclose reach data for the US or all countries, meaning total exposure was likely higher.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: The 2,563-account figure is a documented floor, not a ceiling, given the missing US reach data — actual exposure of illegal CSAM advertising content to real users was likely significantly larger than what TTP could measure.
insights.locator: Although many of the ads, according to Meta's data

insights.claim: After WIRED contacted Meta, researchers discovered around 30 additional abusive ads beyond the initial roughly two dozen found, with many of these newly discovered ads having been published after WIRED first asked Meta about the content — meaning some of the worst instances the researchers had seen were live and actively being shown to accounts at the very time they were being investigated.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: New CSAM ads continued to be published and served even after Meta was directly alerted to the problem by a journalist, indicating the company's detection and prevention systems were failing in real time, not just retrospectively — a stronger case for systemic ad-review failure than a backlog issue.
insights.locator: Many of these ads had been published after WIRED first asked Meta

insights.claim: TTP director Katie Paul says the cache included some ads that appeared identical to ads Meta had previously removed for policy violations, raising the question of how Meta's own systems could identify identical ads via prior removals yet fail to proactively remove the recurring duplicates.
insights.speaker: Katie Paul (via Matt Burgess)
insights.so_what: Evidence of repeat/duplicate ad content evading removal despite matching prior violations suggests Meta's content-matching enforcement (e.g., hash-matching for known violating content) is either not applied to ads or is being circumvented — a specific, actionable engineering/policy gap.
insights.quote: This raises significant questions about how seriously Meta is taking child exploitation in paid advertisements if its own systems can identify identical ads but it does not remove those identical ads for CSAM material.
insights.locator: The TTP's Paul says that within the cache of ads

themes.theme: Meta's response and the broader nudify-app ecosystem

insights.claim: Meta says the majority of the ads had minimal reach and many were disabled before WIRED shared them, and states many of the ads predate a new AI technology the company recently launched to better detect and block violating ads at upload; Meta also says it removed over 36 million pieces of child sexual exploitation content last year and has taken legal action against nudify app developers.
insights.speaker: Meta spokesperson (via Matt Burgess)
insights.so_what: Meta's own defense (that new AI detection tech only recently launched) is undercut by the article's own finding that new violating ads continued to appear after WIRED's outreach, indicating the newly launched detection system has not closed the gap it was built to close.
insights.quote: Sexual exploitation is horrific, and we work aggressively to keep it off our platform. The majority of these ads had minimal reach and many were disabled before WIRED shared them.

insights.claim: Several of the Meta ads found by TTP linked to an app called MaskAI, tied to a Chinese software developer, which showed no nudity before download but, once opened, exclusively contained AI-generated pornography with face-swap features letting users insert real people's faces into sexual situations; after WIRED's inquiry, Apple removed MaskAI from the App Store for violating its anti-nudification policies.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: Illustrates a cross-platform enforcement gap: an app with hidden illegal functionality passed Apple's App Store review and was actively advertised via Meta's ad network, requiring a journalist's direct outreach to trigger removal from either platform — evidence that automated review at both major gatekeepers failed here.
insights.locator: Several of the Meta ads found by the TTP researchers

insights.claim: In one traced case, the advertiser behind an ad depicting a girl in a sexual position was a Chinese firm called Meet Social, which was previously one of Meta's authorized ad resellers handling ads in China (where Meta's platforms are themselves blocked), and which a 2019 New York Times profile said published thousands of Facebook ads per day and expected more than $1 billion in sales.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: A high-volume, high-revenue authorized Meta ad reseller based in China — a market where Meta itself is banned — was the traced source of at least one CSAM-linked ad, highlighting a structural risk in Meta's reseller-partner model for markets it cannot directly police.
insights.locator: the TTP researchers say Meta's data indicates the advertiser

insights.claim: Alexios Mantzarlis, cofounder of Indicator and a former Google trust-and-safety worker, says he has personally found and reported more than 25,000 ads for AI nudifiers on Meta's platforms in recent years; Meta has previously said it took down more than 344,000 nudifier ads and sued a Hong Kong company linked to a set of nudifier platforms, but Mantzarlis says the actors behind these networks are well-equipped to keep creating new advertiser accounts and domains, similar to techniques used by scam networks.
insights.speaker: Alexios Mantzarlis (via Matt Burgess)
insights.so_what: A 344,000-ad takedown figure sounds large in isolation, but paired with an independent researcher's 25,000+ individually reported ads and an explicit description of the abuse networks as adaptive and scam-like, it indicates a persistent, self-replenishing adversarial ecosystem that enforcement has not meaningfully shrunk.
insights.quote: The actors on the other side are clearly well-equipped to create new advertiser accounts and new domains so that they can keep going, leveraging the same techniques used by scam networks.
insights.locator: Alexios Mantzarlis, cofounder of digital deception publication Indicator

insights.claim: This is the second time in recent weeks that paid ads linked to child sexual abuse material have been found on Meta's platforms, following an early-July BBC investigation that found Instagram running ads promoting the sale of what appeared to be child sexual abuse material in India, using terms like 'rape video' and linking to Telegram channels selling the content.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: Two independent investigations in close succession finding CSAM-linked paid ads on Meta's platforms establish a repeated pattern rather than an isolated failure, strengthening the case for systemic ad-review deficiencies rather than a one-off lapse.
